meta.title: European Parliament elections, 1979–2024
sources: Wikipedia election infoboxes and group-composition tables for the 1979–2024 European Parliament elections (user-supplied extract, July 2026)
meta.note: Group compositions are those at or immediately after each Parliament's constitutive session, from the source's composition tables; Non-Inscrits computed as the remainder of the chamber where the source lists groups only. Vote shares are EU-wide shares for the parties that formed each group, where the source reports them.

eras.label: The Community years
eras.blurb: The world's first directly elected transnational parliament, chosen by nine countries in 1979 and twelve by 1994. It began with few real powers, a chamber of national delegations grouped loosely into families, and turnout that started at 62% and never stopped falling.

eras.label: Enlargement & empowerment
eras.blurb: Maastricht, Amsterdam and Lisbon made the Parliament a genuine co-legislator just as the Union grew from 15 states to 27. The centre-right EPP overtook the Socialists in 1999 and has been the largest group ever since, while turnout slid below 50% and kept going.

eras.label: The polycrisis parliaments
eras.blurb: Three elections fought amid the euro crisis, migration, Brexit, a pandemic and war in Ukraine. The Spitzenkandidat experiment made and then unmade itself, the grand-coalition duopoly lost its combined majority for the first time in 2019, turnout finally rebounded, and the radical right kept growing until, by 2024, it filled three separate groups.

elections.summary: The first direct election to any transnational assembly in history: 110 million voters in nine countries chose 410 MEPs, replacing the appointed delegates who had sat since 1958. The Socialists formed the largest group, but the chamber elected the liberal Simone Veil, Auschwitz survivor and French health minister, as its first president.

Greece's accession brought the electorate to ten countries. The Socialists consolidated their lead, but the sensation was Jean-Marie Le Pen's Front National winning 10 far-right seats in France and founding the European Right group, the radical right's first parliamentary bridgehead in the chamber.

Spain and Portugal's first full European election, held as the Berlin Wall entered its final months. The Socialists won a third straight victory, and the green wave arrived: 30 MEPs formed the first Green group after breakthroughs in Britain (15% of the vote and no seats, courtesy of first-past-the-post), France and Germany.

groups.name: European Liberal Democrat and Reform Party

elections.summary: The first post-Maastricht election returned the Socialists' largest-ever group, 198 seats, in a chamber enlarged for German reunification. Silvio Berlusconi, Italy's brand-new Prime Minister, exported his party wholesale as Forza Europa, the first group built from a single national party.

elections.summary: Weeks after the Santer Commission resigned en masse over fraud allegations, a Parliament that had just flexed real power saw the EPP overtake the Socialists for the first time since 1979, a lead it has never surrendered. Turnout fell below 50% for the first time.

groups.name: Alliance of Liberals and Democrats for Europe
Union for Europe of the Nations

elections.summary: The first election after the big-bang enlargement: 342 million eligible voters in 25 countries, the largest transnational vote ever held to that point. Ten mostly ex-communist new member states elected their first MEPs, turnout hit a new low of 45%, and UKIP's 12 seats previewed a rising eurosceptic tide.

groups.name: Progressive Alliance of Socialists and Democrats
Alliance of Liberals and Democrats for Europe

elections.summary: Held in the trough of the financial crisis, the election punished governing socialists rather than incumbents generally: the EPP won decisively while the S&D fell to its worst result yet. David Cameron's Conservatives walked out of the EPP to found the ECR, and Jerzy Buzek of Poland became the first president of the chamber from the former eastern bloc.

countries.note: Countries are grouped by the European group each national party sat with before the election, as the source presents them; the source table sums to 737 against the chamber's 736 full members.

elections.summary: The first election fought under the Spitzenkandidat system, in which the lead candidate of the winning family claims the Commission presidency: the EPP's Jean-Claude Juncker duly got the job over David Cameron's objections. Eurosceptic insurgents topped the poll outright in Britain (UKIP), France (Front National) and Denmark, the first time anti-EU parties had won national first places at a European election. Group seat totals are those at the Parliament's constitutive session.

groups.name: Progressive Alliance of Socialists and Democrats

elections.summary: Turnout rose for the first time in the Parliament's history, above 50%, in a contest framed as pro- versus anti-European. The EPP–S&D grand coalition lost its combined majority for the first time since 1979, liberals and greens surged, and Britain elected MEPs it would withdraw within a year. The Spitzenkandidat system collapsed: the European Council bypassed every lead candidate to nominate Ursula von der Leyen.

elections.summary: The first election of the post-Brexit Union returned a Parliament shifted rightward: the radical right now filled three groups, with Viktor Orbán's new Patriots for Europe becoming the third-largest, while the Greens and liberals gave back their 2019 gains. The EPP alone gained seats among the big groups, and Ursula von der Leyen was confirmed for a second Commission term.
